label: Lemma:Apolarity
title: Lemma
body_md:
\cite[Lemma 1.15]{IK99}\label{Lemma:Apolarity}  \rm(Apolarity Lemma)
      Let $\mathbb{X}=\{P_1, \ldots, P_r\} \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ be a set of points. Then  $F = \sum_{i=1}^r\alpha_i L_i^d$ for some $\alpha_i \in \mathbb{C}$ if and only if $I(\mathbb{X}) \subset F^{\perp}$ where $L_i$ is the linear form corresponding to the point $P_i$ for $1 \leq i \leq r.$

label: Thm:Ecomputability
title: Theorem

label: Lemma:ColonRegularSequence
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $g\in (J+ (ha)) :(h)$. Therefore
    $gh \in J+ (ha)$. That is, 
    $gh = b' + a'ha$ for some $b' \in J$ and $a' \in T.$
    Since $h$ is a nonzerodivisor on $T/J$, we obtain
    $g-a'a \in J$. 
    Hence $g = b+a'a$ for some $b \in J$. Therefore $g \in (J:(h)) +(a)$. Verifying the other way containment is an easy check.
head: environment

label: Theorem:Rank CI non reduced
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{Theorem:Rank CI non reduced}
    Let $F^\perp = (f_0, f_1, \ldots,f_n) \subseteq T$ be a complete intersection.
    Let $\deg f_i = a_i$ and assume that  $a_0 \leqslant a_1\leqslant \ldots \leqslant a_n$. 
    Assume that $f_i$ is non-reduced for some $i$. Then
    \[
    \operatorname{Rk}(F) \geqslant \frac{1}{a_k}\prod\nolimits_{i=0}^n a_i\,,
    \] 
    where $k$ is the smallest such that $f_k$ is not reduced.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\noindent   
    Let $f_k =h^2 g$ and $I=(h)$ with $\deg h \geq 1$. Suppose $\mathbb{X}\subset \mathbb P^n$
    is an  apolar set of $F$ such that $I(\mathbb{X})\subset F^\perp$.
    
    First we show that $h$ 
    is not a zero divisor on $T/(I(\mathbb{X}) : I)$. 
    If $h\in F^\perp=(f_0,\ldots,f_n)$, then since ${\rm deg}(h)<{\rm deg}(f_k)$,
    it follows that $f_k = h^2g$ is in the ideal $(f_0,\ldots,f_{k-1})$,
    a contradiction. Thus, $h \notin F^\perp$, hence $h \notin I(\mathbb{X})$.
    Suppose there exists $g_1 \in T$ such that 
    \[\bar{h}\bar{g_1} = \overline{0} \]
    in $T / (I(\mathbb{X}) : I)$,
    then $h^2g_1\in I(\mathbb X)$. Since $I(\mathbb X)$
    is reduced, we get $hg_1\in I(\mathbb X)$, which shows that $g_1 \in (I(\mathbb X):I)$.
    Hence $h$ is not a zero divisor on $T/(I(\mathbb{X}) : I)$.

    Now we apply \cite[Theorem 3.3]{CCCGW18} by taking $I=(h)$ and $t=h$.
    Let 
    $$\tilde{I} = (F^{\perp}:(h)) +(h)\,.$$
    Then we get 
    $$|\mathbb X|\geqslant \frac{1}{{\rm deg}(h)}\sum_{i\geqslant 0} \operatorname{HF}(T/\tilde I, i)\,.$$
    
    Let $J=(f_0,f_1,\ldots, f_{k-1},f_{k+1}, \ldots, f_n)$. 
    Then $F^{\perp} = J+(h^2g)$. Since $f_0,\ldots, f_{k-1}, h, f_{k+1}, \ldots, f_n$ 
    is also a regular sequence, applying Lemma \ref{Lemma:ColonRegularSequence} we obtain
    \begin{align*}
        \tilde{I}&= (F^{\perp}:(h)) +(h)\\
            &=((J+(h^2g)):(h))+(h)\\
            &=((J:(h))+(hg))+(h)\\
            &=(J:(h))+(h)\\
            &=(f_0,\ldots, f_{k-1}, h, f_{k+1}, \ldots, f_n)\,
    \end{align*} 
    as $h$ is regular on $T/J$.
    Hence 
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:e-comp}
    |\mathbb X|\geqslant \frac{1}{{\rm deg}(h)}\sum_{i\geqslant 0} \operatorname{HF}(T/\tilde I, i) = \prod_{i=0, i\neq k}^n \deg f_i  =  \frac{1}{a_k}\prod_{i=0}^n a_i \,. 
    \end{equation}
    This shows that 
    $$\operatorname{Rk}(F) \geqslant  \frac{1}{a_k}\prod_{i=0}^n a_i\,.$$
    This completes the proof of the Proposition.
head: environment

label: upper bound k-1 reduced
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{upper bound k-1 reduced}
    Let $F^\perp = (f_0, f_1, \ldots,f_n) \subseteq T$ be a complete intersection.
    Let $\deg f_i = a_i$ and assume that  $a_0 \leqslant a_1\leqslant \ldots \leqslant a_n$. 
    For some  $0 \leq k \leq n$, if $V(f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_{k-1})\subset \mathbb P^n$ is a reduced subscheme, then 
    $$\operatorname{Rk}(F) \leqslant  \frac{1}{a_k}\prod\nolimits_{i=0}^n a_i\,.$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $Y=V(f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_{k-1})$ and  
    let $Z\subset Y$ denote the singular locus. 
    If $k=0$ then we mean $Y=\mathbb P^n$ and so 
    $Z=\emptyset$. 
    
    By our hypothesis, we get that 
    ${\rm dim}(Y)=n-k$ and ${\rm dim}(Z)\leqslant n-k-1$. 
    Consider the space of forms $(F^{\perp})_{a_n}$. This defines a base point free 
    linear system on $Y$ and so also on $Z$. 
    Let $U:=Y\setminus Z$. For general $g_n$ in $(F^{\perp})_{a_n}$ we see that 
    $U\cap V(g_n)$ is smooth and ${\rm dim}(Z\cap V(g_n))\leqslant n-k-2$.
    Next consider the space of forms ${(F^{\perp})}_{a_{n-1}}$. This defines a base point 
    free linear system on $Y\cap V(g_n)$. For general $g_{n-1}$ in ${(F^{\perp})}_{a_{n-1}}$ we see that 
    $U\cap V(g_n,g_{n-1})$ is smooth and ${\rm dim}(Z\cap V(g_n,g_{n-1}))\leqslant n-k-3$.
    Proceeding in this fashion we see that 
    $U\cap V(g_n,\ldots,g_{k+1})$ is smooth and 
    ${\rm dim}(Z\cap V(g_n,\ldots,g_{k+1}))\leqslant -1$, that is, it is empty.
    It follows that 
    $$\mathbb X:=V(f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_{k-1},g_{k+1},\ldots,g_n)\subset \mathbb P^n$$
    is a smooth subscheme of dimension 0. Clearly, $I(\mathbb X)\subset F^\perp$ and 
    $|\mathbb X|=\frac{1}{a_k}\prod\nolimits_{i=0}^n a_i$. Since $\operatorname{Rk}(F)\leqslant |\mathbb X|$, 
    this completes the proof of the Proposition.
head: environment

label: thm2
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm2}
    Let $F^\perp = (f_0, f_1, \ldots,f_n) \subseteq T$ be a complete intersection.
    Let $\deg f_i = a_i$ and assume that  $a_0 \leqslant a_1\leqslant \ldots \leqslant a_n$. 
    Assume that $f_i$ is non-reduced for some $i$. Let $k$ be the smallest 
    such that $f_k$ is not reduced and assume that the subscheme 
    $V(f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_{k-1})\subset \mathbb P^n$
    is reduced for $0 \leq k \leq n$. Then $\operatorname{Rk}(F)=\frac{1}{a_k}\prod\nolimits_{i=0}^n a_i$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
This follows from Proposition \ref{Theorem:Rank CI non reduced}
    and Proposition \ref{upper bound k-1 reduced}.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The hypothesis that $V(f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_{k-1})\subset \mathbb P^n$ is a reduced subscheme
    is necessary. See Example \ref{counterexample}.
head: environment

label: thm1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm1}
    Let $F^\perp=(f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_n)$ be a complete intersection. 
    Let $a_i={\rm deg}(f_i)$ and assume that $a_0\leqslant a_1\leqslant \ldots\leqslant a_n$.
    If the subscheme $V(f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_{n-1})\subset \mathbb P^n$
    is reduced, then 
    $\operatorname{Rk}(F)=\prod\nolimits_{i=0}^{n-1}a_i$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
From Proposition \ref{upper bound k-1 reduced} it follows that 
    $\operatorname{Rk}(F)\leqslant \prod\nolimits_{i=0}^{n-1}a_i$. 
    Since $F^{\perp}$ is generated in degree $a_n$, 
    by \cite[Proposition 1]{RS11} we have any scheme apolar 
    to $F$ has length at least  $ \prod\nolimits_{i=0}^{n-1}a_i.$ 
    Hence $\operatorname{Rk}(F)\geqslant \prod\nolimits_{i=0}^{n-1}a_i$.  
    This completes the proof of the Theorem.
head: environment

label: Thm:MainRank
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We divide the proof into the following cases: 
    \newline\noindent{\underline{\it Case}}(i). Assume $(X_0^{a_0}+G)$ has a multiple factor. In this case, all the generators of $F^{\perp}$ are non-reduced. By applying Theorem \ref{thm1} with $k=0$ case, we obtain the result. 
    \newline\noindent{\underline{\it Case}}(ii). Assume $(X_0^{a_0}+G)$ does not have a multiple factor. In this case, we consider the following sub-cases:
    \newline{\underline{\it Case}}(ii.a). Suppose $a_0 \leq a_1$. Since $(X_0^{a_0}+G)$  is square-free, $V(X_0^{a_0}+G)$ is reduced. Moreover, $X_1^{a_1}$ is non-reduced. Hence, we apply Theorem \ref{thm2} with $k=1$ case, we obtain
    \[
    \operatorname{Rk} F = {a_0{\displaystyle\prod_{j=2}^n a_j}}.
    \]
    {\underline{\it Case}}(ii.b). Suppose $a_0 > a_1$. In this case, the least degree generator of $F^{\perp}$ is $X_1^{a_1}$ which is non-reduced. Hence, we apply Theorem \ref{thm2} with $k=0$ case, we obtain \[
    \operatorname{Rk} F = {a_0{\displaystyle\prod_{j=2}^n a_j}}.
    \]
head: environment

title: Example
body_md: Consider $I=(X^2+Y^2+Z^2, Y^3, Z^3)$ and $F= x^5-5x^3y^2-5x^3z^2+15xy^2z^2$.  By Macaulay2 we verify that $F^{\perp} = I.$ Hence, by Corollary \ref{Thm:MainRank} we obtain $\operatorname{Rk} F = 6.$

label: Thm:Shibata
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Thm:Shibata}
    Let  $S=\mathbb{C}[x_0, x_1]$, and $T=\mathbb{C}[X_0, X_1]$ be the standard graded polynomial rings. Let 
    \[
    F=x_0^{a_0}x_1^{a_1}(x_0^{b_0}-x_1^{b_0})
    \]
    where $b_0, a_0,a_1 \in \mathbb{N}$ with $b_0\geq 1,$ $0 \leq  a_0\leq a_1.$
    Let \[
    v = \min \{i \mid a_0+1 \leq i b_0\}, \quad w = \min\{i \mid a_1+1 \leq i b_0\}.
    \]
    Then 
    \[
    F^{\perp} = \begin{dcases}
        \left(X_0^{a_0+b_0+1}, \, M=\sum_{i=0}^vX_0^{ib_0}X_1^{a_1+1-ib_0}\right) \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad\quad \quad \quad \quad \quad\textrm{  if } v<w; \\
        \left( P= \sum_{i=0}^v X_0^{ib_0}X_1^{(v-i)b_0}, \, Q= \sum_{i=0}^{v-1} X_0^{a_0+1-(v-1-i)b_0}X_1^{a_1+1-ib_0} \right) \quad \quad\textrm{if } v=w.
    \end{dcases}
    \]

label: Thm:Binary
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: lem:binary
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:binary}
    If $F \in \mathbb{C}[x_0,x_1]_{d}$, 
    then ${F}^{\perp} = (g_0, g_1)$ where $\deg (g_0) \leqslant \deg (g_1)$ and 
    $g_1=\ell^2 g$ for some linear form 
    $\ell$, $g\in \mathbb{C}[x_0,x_1]$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It is a well-known fact that for $F \in \mathbb{C}[x_0,x_1]_{d}$, 
    we have ${F}^{\perp} = (g_0, g_1)$ such that $\deg (g_0) \leqslant \deg (g_1)$. We want to show that the generator $g_1$ can be replaced by a polynomial which is not reduced. 
    Since $g_0, g_1$ is a regular sequence, choose a linear form $\ell_0\mid g_0$ and $\ell_0 \nmid g_1.$ Let $\tilde {g_0} =\ell_0^{\deg g_1 - \deg g_0} g_0$. For any $\lambda \in \mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$, we have  $h = \tilde {g_0} - \lambda g_1 \in F^{\perp}$ and $F^{\perp} = (g_0, h)$.
    
    We now find $\lambda \in  \mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$ such that $h$ is not reduced.
    Consider the map $\varphi: \mathbb P^1\to \mathbb P^1$
defined by $\varphi([a:b])= [\tilde {g_0}(a,b):g_1(a,b)]$. Note that $\varphi$ is a proper map since the graphs of $\tilde {g_0}, g_1$ are closed. Moreover, for each point $P=[u:v] \in \mathbb{P}^1$, the fibre at $P$, $\varphi^{-1}(P)=V_+(v\tilde{g_0} -ug_1)$ is finite where $V_+(v\tilde{g_0} -ug_1)$ denotes the projective zero set of the homogeneous polynomial $v\tilde{g_0} -ug_1$. Hence $\varphi$ is a finite map of degree equals to $\deg g_1$.  By Hurwitz formula, see \cite[Chapter 4, Corollary 2.4]{Ha},
the number of ramification points of this map is nonzero, and we can choose a ramification point $P$ such that $g_1(P) \neq 0.$ 
We now claim that $h$ is not reduced for $\lambda = \frac{\tilde {g_0}(P)}{g_1(P)}$. Note that \[\varphi^{-1}([\lambda:1]) = V_+(\tilde{g_0} - \lambda g_1) = V_+(h).\]
Since $P=[u:v]$ is ramified, we get $\mid \varphi^{-1}([\frac{\tilde {g_0}(P)}{g_1(P)}:1])\mid < \deg \varphi.$ Hence $\mid V_+(h) \mid < \deg g_1$. Therefore $h$ has a multiple factor $\ell = vx+uy$. i.e., we can assume $g_1= h =\ell^2g$ for some $g \in \mathbb{C}[x,y]$.
head: environment

label: EQ:rkFormula
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma \ref{lem:binary} assume $F_1^{\perp} = (g_0, g_1)$ with $g_1 = \ell^2g$ with $\deg(g_0) \leq \deg(g_1)$. Then
    \[
    F^{\perp} = (g_0, \ell^2g, X_2^{a_2+1}, \ldots, X_n^{a_n+1}).
    \]
  We now divide the proof in to following cases and apply Theorem \ref{thm2} to obtain the result. 
  \newline \noindent {\underline {\it Case} (i)}. Suppose $g_0$ is reduced and $\deg g_0 \leq a_2+1.$ Hence $V(g_0)$ is reduced. Note that except $g_0$, all the other generators are non-reduced in $F^{\perp}.$
  Hence by Theorem \ref{thm2} we obtain 
  \[\operatorname{Rk} F = \left(\frac{1}{\min\{a_2+1, \deg g_1\}}\right)\deg g_0 \cdot \deg g_1 \cdot \prod_{i=2}^n(a_i+1). \]
  Since $g_0$ is reduced, $\deg g_0 = \operatorname{Rk} F_1,$ and $\deg g_1 = \deg F_1+2\operatorname{Rk} F_1$. Therefore we obtain
  \begin{align*}
        \operatorname{Rk} F = (\operatorname{Rk} F_1)\cdot \max\{a_2+1, \deg F_1+2-\operatorname{Rk} F_1\} \cdot\left(\prod_{i=3}^n (a_i+1)\right).
    \end{align*}

\noindent {\underline {\it Case} (ii)}. Suppose $g_0$ is reduced and $\deg g_0 > a_2+1.$ In this case the least degree generator of $F^{\perp}$ is $X_2^{a_2+1}$ which is non-reduced. We apply Theorem \ref{thm2} with $k=0$ case to obtain 
\[
\operatorname{Rk} F = \frac{1}{(a_2+1)} \deg g_0 \cdot \deg g_1 \cdot \prod_{i=2}^n(a_i+1).
\]
As in the above case (i), since $g_0$ is reduced, $\operatorname{Rk} F_1 = \deg g_0$ and $\deg g_1 = \deg F_1 + 2 \operatorname{Rk} F_1$ and $\deg g_1 \geq \deg g_0 > a_2+1.$ Hence we obtain the Equation \eqref{EQ:rkFormula}.

\noindent{\underline {\it Case} (iii)} Assume $g_0$ is non-reduced. In this case, all the generators of $F^{\perp}$ are non-reduced. 
By applying Theorem \ref{thm2} with $k=0$ case, we obtain
\[
\operatorname{Rk} F = \left(\frac{1}{\min\{a_2+1, \deg g_0\}}\right) \deg g_1 \cdot \prod_{i=2}^n(a_i+1).
\]
Moreover, $\operatorname{Rk} F_1= \deg g_1$ and $\deg g_0 = \deg F_1 +2 -\operatorname{Rk} F_1.$ Substituting in the Equation above, we obtain the result.

label: Thm:BinomialAnnihilator
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Thm:BinomialAnnihilator}
 Let  
\[ F = x_0^{a_0}\cdots x_k^{a_k}(x_0^{b_0} - x_1^{b_1}\cdots x_k^{b_k})\]
be a binomial form with all $b_i \neq 0$ such that $\sum_{i=1}^n b_i = b_0$ and $k \geq 2,$ and $a_i \geq 0.$ If there exists an integer $1 \leq i \leq k$ with $a_i < q b_i$ where $q = \lfloor{\frac{a_0+1}{b_0}}\rfloor$, then
\[
F^{\perp} = (X_0^{a_0+1}+G, X_1^{a_1+b_1+1}, \ldots , X_k^{a_k+b_k+1}) 
\]
where $G = \sum_{j=1}^m (X_1^{b_1}\cdots X_k^{b_k})^{j} X_0^{a_0+1 - jb_0}$ with 
$m = \min \{\lfloor {\frac{a_i}{b_i}} \rfloor \mid 1 \leq i \leq k\}.$
head: environment

label: Thm:BinomialRank
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Thm:BinomialRank}
    Let $F =x_0^{a_0}x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_n^{a_n}(x_0^{b_0} - x_1^{b_1}\cdots x_n^{b_n})$.  Write $F = F_1F_2$ where $F_1 = x_0^{a_0}x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_k^{a_k}(x_0^{b_0} - x_1^{b_1}\cdots x_k^{b_k})$ a binomial with  $b_i \neq 0$ for $1 \leq i \leq k $, $b_{k+1}= \cdots = b_n = 0$, and $F_2 = x_{k+1}^{a_{k+1}}\cdots x_n^{a_n}$ for some $1 \leq k \leq n$, and  $a_{k+1} \leq \cdots \leq a_n$. 
    \newline If $2 \leq k \leq n$, and $F_1$ satisfies conditions as in Theorem \ref{Thm:BinomialAnnihilator}, then  
    \[
    \operatorname{Rk} F = \frac{(a_0+1)}{\lambda} \prod_{i=1}^k (a_i+b_i+1)\prod_{i=k+1}^n (a_i+1) 
    \]
    where $\lambda = \min\{\{a_0+1, a_k+1\} \cup \{a_i+b_i+1 \mid 1 \leq i \leq k\}\}$.

label: Thm:ProductBinary
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Thm:ProductBinary}
    If $F=F_1F_2$ such that $F_1 \in (T_1)_{d_1}$, $F_2 \in (T_2)_{d_2}$ as defined above,
    then 
    \[
    \operatorname{Rk} (F) = (\operatorname{Rk} (F_1))\cdot (\operatorname{Rk} (F_2)) \cdot\max\{d_1+2-\operatorname{Rk} (F_1), d_2+2 -\operatorname{Rk} (F_2)\}.
    \]
head: environment
name: Waring rank of product of binary forms

title: Proof
body_md:
Without loss of generality, assume that ${\rm deg}(g_0) \leqslant {\rm deg}(h_0)$.
We prove the result by considering the following cases.
\begin{enumerate}[label={\rm (\Alph*)}]
    \item If $g_0$ is non-reduced. 
    Applying Theorem \ref{thm2} with $k=0$ we get
    \[
    \operatorname{Rk} (F) ={\rm deg}(g_1){\rm deg}(h_0){\rm deg}(h_1).
    \]
    \item If $g_0$ is reduced, 
    ${\rm deg}(g_0)\leqslant {\rm deg}(g_1)\leqslant {\rm deg}(h_0)$. 
    By Lemma \ref{lem:binary}, $g_1$ is non-reduced, and 
    applying Theorem \ref{thm2} with $k=1$ we get 
    \[
    \operatorname{Rk} (F) ={\rm deg}(g_0){\rm deg}(h_0){\rm deg}(h_1).
    \]
    \item If $g_0$ is reduced, 
    ${\rm deg}(g_0)\leqslant {\rm deg}(h_0)< {\rm deg}(g_1)$, 
    and $h_0$ is non-reduced.
    Applying Theorem \ref{thm2} with $k=1$ we get     
    \[
    \operatorname{Rk} (F) ={\rm deg}(g_0){\rm deg}(g_1){\rm deg}(h_1).
    \]
    \item If $g_0$ is reduced, 
    ${\rm deg}(g_0)\leqslant {\rm deg}(h_0)< {\rm deg}(g_1)$, 
    and $h_0$ is reduced.
    By Lemma \ref{lem:binary}, both $g_1$ 
    and $h_1$ are non-reduced. 
    Applying Theorem \ref{thm2} with $k=2$ we get 
    \[
    \operatorname{Rk} (F) ={\rm deg}(g_0){\rm deg}(h_0)\cdot {\rm max}\{{\rm deg}(g_1),{\rm deg}(h_1)\}.
    \]
\end{enumerate}

Using \eqref{eq:Sylvesters algo} we compute the entries
in the following table. Note that 
if $\operatorname{Rk} (F_2) = \deg (h_i)$, then $d_2+2-\operatorname{Rk} (F_2) = \deg h_{1-i}$.

\begin{center}
{\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}[t]{|p{.5cm}|p{5cm}|p{1.2cm}|p{1.2cm}|p{6cm}|}
		\hline
		   & \bf Hypothesis & $\mathbf{Rk}(F_1)$ & $\mathbf{Rk}(F_2)$ & $\mathbf{max}\{d_1+2-\mathrm{rk} F_1, d_2+2 -\mathrm{rk} F_2\}$ \\ \hline  
        (A) & \vspace{-1ex}
        \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, nosep]\setlength{\itemsep}{0pt}
        \item $g_0$ is non-reduced
        \end{itemize} & $\deg (g_1)$ & $\deg (h_i)$ & $\max\{\deg (g_0), \deg (h_{1-i})\} = \deg (h_{1-i})$ \\ \hline  
        (B) & \vspace{-1ex}
        \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, nosep]\setlength{\itemsep}{0pt}
                \item $g_0$ is reduced
                \item $\mathrm{deg}(g_0)\leqslant \mathrm{deg}(g_1)\leqslant \mathrm{deg}(h_0)$
              \end{itemize} & $\deg (g_0)$ & $\deg (h_i)$ &$\max\{\deg (g_1), \deg (h_{1-i})\} = \deg (h_{1-i})$  \\ \hline  
        (C) & \vspace{-1ex}
        \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, nosep]\setlength{\itemsep}{0pt}
                \item $g_0$ is reduced
                \item $\mathrm{deg}(g_0)\leqslant \mathrm{deg}(h_0)< \mathrm{deg}(g_1)$
                \item $h_0$ is non-reduced
              \end{itemize} &$\deg (g_0)$  & $\deg (h_1)$& $\max\{\deg (g_1), \deg (h_0)\} = \deg (g_1)$  \\ \hline  
        (D) & \vspace{-1ex}
        \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, nosep]\setlength{\itemsep}{0pt}
                \item $g_0$ is reduced
                \item $\mathrm{deg}(g_0)\leqslant \mathrm{deg}(h_0)< \mathrm{deg}(g_1)$
                \item $h_0$ is reduced
              \end{itemize}\vspace{-2ex} &$\deg (g_0)$  & $\deg (h_0)$& $\max\{\deg (g_1), \deg (h_1)\}$  \\ \hline  
\end{tabular}
}
\end{center}
One easily checks that in all cases 
$\operatorname{Rk} (F) = (\operatorname{Rk} (F_1))\cdot (\operatorname{Rk} (F_2)) \cdot\max\{d_1+2-\operatorname{Rk} (F_1), d_2+2 -\operatorname{Rk} (F_2)\}$. This completes
the proof of the Theorem.
head: environment

label: counterexample
title: Example
body_md:
\label{counterexample}
Consider $I= (Y^2-Z^2, XY, X^5-Z^5) \subset T=\mathbb{C}[X,Y,Z]$. 
Note that $I$ is an Artinian complete intersection ideal. Hence, 
there exists a homogeneous form $F$ such that $F^{\perp}=I$. Moreover, each of the generators of $F^{\perp}$ is reduced(does not have a multiple factor), but $V(Y^2-Z^2, XY)$ is non-reduced.
We show that $4 < \operatorname{Rk} (F) \leqslant 8.$

\begin{proof}
We first show that $\operatorname{Rk} F \geq 4$. 
Let $\mathbb{X}$ be such that $I(\mathbb{X}) \subseteq F^{\perp}$.
Since $I(\mathbb X)$ is a radical ideal, by \cite{GMR83}, the sequence $(c_0,c_1,\ldots)$ where
\[c_i=\operatorname{HF}(T/I(\mathbb{X}), i)-\operatorname{HF}(T/I(\mathbb{X}), i-1)\]
is the Hilbert function of an Artinian ring. It follows
that 
$$\operatorname{HF}(T/I(\mathbb{X}), i)\geqslant \operatorname{HF}(T/I(\mathbb{X}), i-1)$$
for all $i$. 
Since $I(\mathbb{X}) \subset F^{\perp}$
we obtain 
$$\operatorname{HF}(T/F^{\perp}, i) \leq \operatorname{HF}(T/I(\mathbb{X}), i)$$ 
for all $i$.
Hence, 
$$3 = \operatorname{HF}(T/F^{\perp}, 1) \leq \operatorname{HF}(T/I(\mathbb{X}), 1)\leqslant 3,$$
and 
$$4 = \operatorname{HF}(T/F^{\perp}, 2) \leq \operatorname{HF}(T/I(\mathbb{X}), 2)\,.$$ 
Therefore, $\operatorname{HF}(T/I(\mathbb{X}), i) \geq 4$ for $i \geq 2.$
Recall that $\operatorname{Rk}(F)=\operatorname{HF}(T/I(\mathbb{X}), i)$ for $i\gg 0$.
Thus, $\operatorname{Rk}(F) \geq 4$.

We now claim that $\operatorname{Rk}(F)> 4$.
If not, assume that $\operatorname{Rk}(F)=|\mathbb X|=4$.
As $\operatorname{HF}(T/I(\mathbb{X}), i)$ is eventually constant and equal to 4,
it follows that the Hilbert function of $T/I(\mathbb{X})$ is $(1,3,4,4,\ldots)$.
Hence,  $I(\mathbb{X})_2 = (F^{\perp})_2 = (Y^2-Z^2, XY)$. 
Therefore, $I(\mathbb{X}) \supseteq (Y^2-Z^2, XY)$. Moreover, it is easy to check that the Hilbert function of $T/J$ is also $(1,3,4,4, \ldots )$, where $J=(Y^2-Z^2, XY)$. Hence $I(\mathbb{X}) =(Y^2-Z^2, XY)$ which is a contradiction because  $V(Y^2-Z^2, XY)$ is not reduced.


We give an upper bound by giving an
explicit apolar ideal $I(\mathbb{X}) \subset F^{\perp}$.
Let $I(\mathbb{X}) = (XY,Y(Y^2-Z^2), X^6+Z^4(Y^2-Z^2))$. 
Using Macaulay2 \cite{M2}, it is easy to check that 
$I(\mathbb{X}) \subset F^{\perp}$ and $I(\mathbb{X})$ 
is a radical ideal with $|\mathbb{X}| = 8$. 
Therefore, $\operatorname{Rk} (F) \leqslant 8$.

\end{proof}
